Edgar Whisenant's 1988 booklet gave dates for the rapture in September 1988. Nothing happened, and he moved the date to 1989.
Lindsey's 1980s book is no longer cited for its forecasts, though it sold widely.

Most futurist scholars agree that date setting is wrong and say that failed forecasts by some teachers do not weaken the hope itself. They separate setting dates from noting trends. They warn that the fulfilled view can make Christians careless about watching for Christ's return.
Is the great tribulation a future seven-year period in which the Antichrist makes a covenant with Israel?
The fulfilled reading says no. Matthew 24 mentions no seven years, no covenant with Israel and no Antichrist. It describes Judea before AD 70.

The seven-year idea comes from Daniel 9:27, where "he" confirms a covenant for one "week". Futurists apply this to a future Antichrist after a gap of 2,000 years. The fulfilled reading makes three points. First, Matthew 24:21 says nothing about seven years or a covenant. Second, Daniel 9:27 follows straight from the Messiah being "cut off" (Daniel 9:26). Many older interpreters read the one who "confirms the covenant" as the Messiah himself (compare Matthew 26:28). Third, Jesus tied the great tribulation to the flight from Judea in his own generation (Matthew 24:16, 34). Several dispensational leaders, such as Charles Ryrie and Tim LaHaye, built a complete future scheme on this verse. This reading says the scheme comes from joining texts, not from Matthew 24 itself.
Daniel 9:26-27: the Messiah is cut off, and then the city and sanctuary are destroyed.
Revelation's 42 months (Revelation 11:2; 13:5) are often added to make seven years. The fulfilled reading links them to the Roman war of AD 66-70, which lasted about three and a half years.

Dispensationalists hold that the 70th week of Daniel is still future and that the church will be raptured before it. Historic premillennialists often expect a future tribulation but not a pre-tribulation rapture. Many amillennial scholars see the 70th week as fulfilled in Christ, or as symbolic of the whole church age.
Doesn't "such as has not been since the beginning of the world ... nor ever shall be" prove the tribulation is still future?
No. This is a standard Bible way of stressing a terrible judgment. Ezekiel used the same words for the Babylonian fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC.

In Ezekiel 5:9 God says he will do to Jerusalem what he has never done before and will never do again. That was about Babylon's siege in 586 BC. Yet Jesus said AD 70 would be worse, and futurists expect something worse still. So the words cannot be a strict ranking. They are a Hebrew way of saying "there is nothing like this". The Bible uses the same style often. Both Hezekiah and Josiah are said to have no king like them (2 Kings 18:5; 23:25). Egypt's cry at the last plague was one never heard before or since (Exodus 11:6). Joel uses it for a locust plague (Joel 2:2). Read this way, Matthew 24:21 fits the fall of Jerusalem. It was the greatest disaster in Israel's covenant history.
2 Kings 18:5 and 2 Kings 23:25 each say no king was like Hezekiah, and no king was like Josiah.
Exodus 11:6: a cry in Egypt "such as there has not been, nor shall be any more".

Futurists answer that Jesus adds "nor ever shall be", and that only a worldwide final distress fits this. They link it to Daniel 12:1 and Revelation 7:14. Some evangelical scholars say AD 70 was indeed unequalled for Israel, but Jesus may also look beyond it. Others see a pattern of tribulation through history.
Was the great tribulation local or worldwide?
On the fulfilled reading it was local: it fell on Judea and Jerusalem. The only escape Jesus gives is to flee Judea to the mountains.

Matthew 23 ends with Jesus' judgment on "this generation" and his lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:36-38). Chapter 24 begins with the temple. The tribulation is tied to "those who are in Judea" (Matthew 24:16). It mentions flat roofs, fields, winter and the Sabbath (Matthew 24:17-20). Luke calls it "great distress upon the land and wrath upon this people" (Luke 21:23). The fulfilled reading asks a simple question. If this were a worldwide disaster, how would running to the hills of Judea help? Only people near the temple could "see" the abomination (Matthew 24:15). The word for "land" in Luke 21:23 is often used of the land of Israel. So the tribulation was a judgment on a city and people, not on the whole planet.
Matthew 24:16: the flight is from Judea, which is smaller than the land of Israel as a whole.
Luke 21:24 describes the result: people fall by the sword, are led captive, and Jerusalem is trampled.

Futurists answer that Revelation describes a worldwide tribulation and that Matthew 24 must fit that picture. They say Judea is mentioned because the crisis begins there. Others see Matthew 24:4-14 as worldwide and 15-28 as local, with a final worldwide fulfilment still to come.
Were the courts, synagogues and governors of Mark 13:9 part of the past tribulation?
Yes, on this reading. The Book of Acts records the apostles before councils, beaten in synagogues and standing before governors and kings.

Jesus warned that his disciples would be handed over to councils, beaten in synagogues and brought before governors and kings (Mark 13:9). He gave a similar warning when he first sent out the Twelve (Matthew 10:17-18). This picture fits first-century Judea, where Jewish councils and synagogue discipline still worked under Roman rule. Acts records these things one by one. Peter and John stood before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:1-22; 5:17-40). Saul dragged believers to prison (Acts 8:1-3). Herod killed James (Acts 12:1-2). Paul was beaten and stoned (Acts 14:19; 16:22-23). He stood before Felix, Festus and King Agrippa (Acts 24-26). The fulfilled reading sees the early part of the discourse fulfilled in the apostles' own lives, before the temple fell.
Acts 5:40: the apostles are beaten by the council and told not to speak in Jesus' name.
Acts 25-26: Paul stands before the governor Festus and King Agrippa II.

Most scholars agree these warnings were fulfilled in Acts. Futurists say they also describe a pattern that will return in the end-time. Amillennial scholars see them as true of Christian witness in every age, wherever believers face hostile courts.
How can AD 70 be called the greatest tribulation when later events, such as the Holocaust, killed more people?
The fulfilled reading measures it by covenant meaning and location, not only by numbers. It was the end of the temple and the old covenant order in the land.

This question must be handled with great care and respect. The Nazi murder of about six million Jews was a horrific crime against the Jewish people. No reading of prophecy should treat it as deserved. The fulfilled reading makes a narrower point. Jesus' words concern "those in Judea" (Matthew 24:16) and the temple. In AD 70 the sanctuary, the priesthood and the sacrifices that had stood for centuries were ended. Lamentations 4:6 shows that Scripture weighs a judgment by covenant privilege, not by numbers alone. On this reading, AD 70 is unique because of what ended there. Later suffering of Jews in other lands is not what Jesus was describing. The Holocaust must be seen as human evil, never as divine punishment.
Lamentations 4:6 calls Jerusalem's punishment greater than Sodom's, because of her greater privilege.
AD 70 ended the daily sacrifice in the temple. It has never been restored.

Futurists say the scale of later suffering shows that the greatest tribulation must still be future. Many Jewish and Christian writers reject any reading that links Jewish suffering to divine judgment, and they warn of the long history of Christian contempt. Most Christians today affirm that God has not rejected the Jewish people (Romans 11:1-2).
What does "unless those days had been cut short, no flesh would be saved" mean?
On the fulfilled reading, no one in Judea would have survived if the war had dragged on. God shortened it for the sake of the elect.

Jesus said those days would be cut short "for the sake of the elect" (Matthew 24:22). The fulfilled reading says "flesh" here means the people in the war zone, since the context is Judea (Matthew 24:16). The war lasted from AD 66 to 70. Inside Jerusalem rival rebel leaders fought each other, burned food stores and killed many (Jewish War 5.1.4). The final siege lasted only about five months, from spring to August AD 70. Josephus says Titus wanted to end it quickly. The "elect" are the believers, many of whom had fled, and the remnant God still meant to save. In the Bible "all flesh" often refers to the people in a region, as in Jeremiah 12:12.
Jewish War 5.1.4: the rebel factions burned stores of grain that could have fed the city for years.
Jeremiah 12:12: "no flesh has peace" refers to the land of Judah under judgment.

Futurists read "no flesh" as all humanity and hold that only a global crisis fits this. They say the days are cut short when Christ returns at the end of the seven years. Some scholars see AD 70 as a smaller pattern of the final distress.
What does Luke mean by "great distress upon the land and wrath upon this people"?
It names the land of Israel and the generation living there. Paul uses similar language for the judgment coming on those who opposed the gospel.

Luke 21:23 says there will be great distress "upon the land" and wrath "upon this people". In context, "the land" is Judea and "this people" are those in Jerusalem when the armies surround it (Luke 21:20). Older commentators such as Frederic Godet noted that Paul seems to echo this. In 1 Thessalonians 2:14-16 Paul says those in Judea who killed the Lord and drove out the apostles faced wrath that had come upon them "to the uttermost". The fulfilled reading sees this as one event. Wrath came on that generation in that land when the city fell. This must not be read as God's wrath on Jewish people in every age. Paul himself was a Jew and prayed for his people (Romans 10:1).
1 Thessalonians 2:16: wrath has come upon them "to the uttermost" (or "at last"), written around AD 50.
Luke 23:28: Jesus tells the women of Jerusalem to weep for themselves and their children.

Futurists agree Luke 21:20-24 describes AD 70, but many say the wider discourse moves on to a future time. Some scholars question how to read 1 Thessalonians 2:16 and warn against using it to blame the Jewish people as a whole. Most churches today reject any idea of collective Jewish guilt.
Who were the false christs and false prophets who said "he is in the wilderness" or "in the inner rooms"?
Josephus and Acts name many: Theudas, "the Egyptian", and other wilderness prophets who promised signs before AD 70.

Jesus warned that false christs would point to the wilderness or to secret rooms (Matthew 24:23-26). Several such men appeared before AD 70. Simon the magician was called "the great power of God" (Acts 8:9-10). About AD 45, Theudas promised to part the Jordan, and the Romans killed him (Antiquities 20.5.1; Acts 5:36). An Egyptian prophet led followers to the Mount of Olives, promising Jerusalem's walls would fall (Antiquities 20.8.6). The commander even took Paul for this man (Acts 21:38). Josephus says impostors led crowds into the desert, promising signs of freedom (Jewish War 2.13.4). Paul compared false teachers to Jannes and Jambres, who copied Moses' signs (2 Timothy 3:8; Exodus 7:11). The fulfilled reading says Jesus' warning was exactly fulfilled.
Acts 21:38: "Are you not the Egyptian who ... led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?"
Josephus (Jewish War 2.13.5) says 30,000 followed the Egyptian. Acts gives 4,000, which is likely closer to the truth.

Most scholars agree that such figures appeared in the first century. Futurists say the warning will be fulfilled again, and more fully, under the final false prophet of Revelation 13:13-14. Many interpreters see false christs as a danger in every generation.
What "great signs and wonders" misled people before AD 70?
Josephus reports false prophets who promised rescue in the temple, and omens such as a sword-like star and a comet. Many people trusted these and stayed in the city.

Jesus warned that false prophets would show signs "to mislead, if possible, even the elect" (Matthew 24:24). Josephus says that on the day the temple burned, a false prophet told people to go up to the temple to receive signs of rescue. About 6,000 died in the portico (Jewish War 6.5.2). He says rebel leaders paid many false prophets to tell people to wait for God's help. He also lists omens: a star like a sword over the city, a comet for a year, a heifer that gave birth to a lamb in the temple court, and the eastern gate opening by itself (Jewish War 6.5.3). Some of these reports may have been rumours spread to keep hope alive. Believers who trusted Jesus' words left instead.
Jewish War 6.5.2: about 6,000 people perished after following a false prophet's promise.
Tacitus also reports armies seen in the sky and the temple doors opening (Histories 5.13).

Futurists see Revelation 13:13-14, where fire comes from heaven, as a greater fulfilment still to come. Historians debate how much of Josephus' list is legend. Some interpreters note that Josephus took the omens as real warnings from God, not as false signs.
What does "as the lightning comes from the east and shines to the west" mean?
It means Christ's coming in judgment would be sudden, open and impossible to miss. It would not be a secret in a desert or an inner room.

Jesus contrasts his coming with the false christs (Matthew 24:26-27). They hide in the wilderness or in rooms. His coming is like lightning that everyone sees at once. In the Old Testament, lightning goes with God coming to act. At Sinai there was thunder and lightning, and the people shook (Exodus 19:16; 20:18). God came from Sinai with fire at his right hand (Deuteronomy 33:2). Zechariah says his arrow will go out like lightning (Zechariah 9:14). In none of these did people see God's body. They saw the signs of his action. On the fulfilled reading, Christ came in AD 70 in this sense. He came as judge through the Roman armies, and the event was sudden and public. The nineteenth-century writer J. Stuart Russell read it this way.
Exodus 20:18: the people saw the lightning and stood far off. They knew the Lord had come down.
Zechariah 9:14: "his arrow will go out like lightning" — God acting in war.

Futurists and most historic Christian readers take verse 27 as Christ's visible personal return, which will be seen worldwide. They contrast it with the local events of verses 15-26. Some evangelical scholars see verses 27-31 as a shift from AD 70 to the final coming.
Can God "come" without being physically seen?
Yes. Scripture often says God "comes" when he acts in judgment through events and nations. Jesus also threatened to "come" to churches in Revelation 2-3.

Isaiah 19:1 says the Lord rides on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt. This was fulfilled when Assyria defeated Egypt, not when God appeared in a body. Micah 1:3-5 says the Lord comes down and treads the high places because of Samaria's sin. Psalm 18:9-14 pictures God coming down with darkness and lightning to rescue David. In Revelation, Jesus warns Ephesus, Pergamum and Sardis that he will "come" to them if they do not repent (Revelation 2:5, 16; 3:3). These are not the final return. They are visits in judgment. The fulfilled reading applies this pattern to Matthew 24:27-30. The Son of Man "came" against Jerusalem in AD 70. People did not see his body, but they saw his judgment.
Isaiah 19:1: the Lord "comes to Egypt" riding on a cloud, and its idols tremble.
Revelation 2:5: "I will come to you and remove your lampstand" — a local judgment.

Most interpreters accept these "comings" in judgment. Futurists and many others argue that the New Testament also clearly teaches a final, bodily, visible return (Acts 1:11). They say Matthew 24:27-31 describes that return, not a judgment visit. Partial preterists agree there is a future bodily return, taught in other texts.
Who brought the judgment on Jerusalem: Rome or God?
Both, in the biblical way of speaking. Rome was the tool, but God was the judge, just as he used Assyria and Babylon before.

The Bible often says God uses a nation to judge another. Assyria was "the rod of my anger" (Isaiah 10:5-6). The Lord gave Judah's king into Nebuchadnezzar's hand (Daniel 1:2). Isaiah asks who gave Jacob to the plunderers and answers, "Was it not the Lord?" (Isaiah 42:24-25). On the road to the cross, Jesus told the women of Jerusalem to weep for their children. He said people would ask the mountains to fall on them (Luke 23:28-30). Revelation 6:16-17 uses the same words, as people hide from "the wrath of the Lamb". The fulfilled reading links the two passages. The Lamb's wrath fell on the generation that rejected him, and Titus' legions carried it out. This reading also uses the passage to argue that Revelation was written before AD 70.
Isaiah 10:5-6: Assyria is sent against a godless nation to take plunder.
Hosea 10:8 is the source of "say to the mountains, Cover us", spoken of Samaria's fall in 722 BC.

Most scholars accept that God uses nations to judge. Many date Revelation to about AD 95 under Domitian, citing Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3), and so read Revelation 6 as future. Futurists see the sixth seal as the final day of wrath. Some evangelical scholars see AD 70 as a preview of that day.
What does "wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather" mean?
It is a proverb of judgment. Where there is a dead body, scavengers come. On this reading, Jerusalem was the corpse and the Roman armies were the birds.

The Greek word in Matthew 24:28 can mean eagle or vulture. Here, gathering at a corpse, it means birds of prey. Jeremiah used this picture when he warned Judah. He stood in the temple gate and told the people not to trust in "the temple of the Lord" (Jeremiah 7:2-4). He said the temple had become a den of robbers (Jeremiah 7:11) and that their bodies would be food for birds (Jeremiah 7:33; 19:7). Jesus repeated much of this. He called the temple a den of robbers (Matthew 21:13). He spoke of "this generation" as Jeremiah spoke of "the generation of his wrath" (Jeremiah 7:29). On the fulfilled reading, the corpse is the city that had rejected its life-giver, and the birds are Rome's legions. The legions marched under eagle standards.
Jeremiah 7:33: "the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the sky".
Deuteronomy 28:49 warns of a nation "as swift as the eagle flies" coming against a disobedient Israel.

Futurists usually see the saying as describing the final battle, linking it to the birds of Revelation 19:17-21. Others read it as a general proverb: judgment comes where it is deserved. Many note that the Roman eagle link is possible but not certain, since the word also means vulture.
What are "the times of the Gentiles" in Luke 21:24?
It is the period during which Gentile powers would trample Jerusalem. Readers disagree about whether it ended in AD 70 or still continues.

Jesus said Jerusalem would be "trampled underfoot by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:24). Daniel 2 and 7 show four Gentile kingdoms ruling over God's people, the last being widely taken as Rome. The fulfilled reading links this to Revelation 11:2, where the holy city is trampled for 42 months. This matches the length of the Roman war of AD 66-70. On this view the trampling was the siege and its aftermath, and the "times" were the set time of Rome's work of judgment. Others in the same tradition think "until" points to a longer period that will end at a future time. All agree that the verse begins with AD 70.
Revelation 11:2: the court is given to the nations, who trample the holy city for 42 months.
The Roman war against Judea began in spring AD 67 under Vespasian and ended with the city's fall in August-September AD 70.

Futurists see the times of the Gentiles as a long period from Babylon's conquest until Christ's return. Some pointed to Israel's capture of Jerusalem's Old City in 1967 as a sign it is ending. Many scholars connect it with "the fullness of the Gentiles" (Romans 11:25), leading to a future turning of Israel.
If the great tribulation is past, will Christians today still face tribulation?
Yes. Jesus promised his people trouble in every age, and he gives them the strength to overcome it. What is past is that one judgment on Jerusalem.

Jesus said, "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). Paul taught that "through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22). Believers today suffer in many countries for their faith. The fulfilled reading does not make light of this. It only says that the "great tribulation" of Matthew 24:21 was a specific event that ended in AD 70. This view also rejects the idea that believers will be taken out of the world before trouble comes. Jesus prayed not that his people be taken out of the world but that they be kept from evil (John 17:15). The church is called to stand firm in hardship, not to wait for escape.
Revelation 1:9: John is the readers' "brother and companion in the tribulation".
Hebrews 10:32-34 describes believers who endured insults, prison and loss of property.

Pre-tribulation believers agree that Christians face tribulation now. They separate this from the future wrath of the seven-year period, from which they believe the church is spared (1 Thessalonians 5:9). Post-tribulation premillennialists expect the church to go through a future great tribulation.
Will giant hailstones literally fall on the earth, as Revelation 16:21 describes?
The fulfilled reading sees the hail as a picture of judgment drawn from the plagues of Egypt and from Joshua's battles, not as a forecast of 50-pound ice blocks.

Revelation 16:21 speaks of hailstones weighing about a talent, which is perhaps 30-45 kilograms. In 1989 one well-known pastor asked readers to imagine 50-pound chunks of ice ripping through roofs. The fulfilled reading starts with the Old Testament. Hail was the seventh plague on Egypt (Exodus 9:23-25). God threw down hailstones on Israel's enemies (Joshua 10:11). Ezekiel promised great hailstones on Gog (Ezekiel 38:22). In each case hail is God's weapon against those who oppose him. Revelation 16 copies the Exodus plagues on purpose, with water to blood, darkness and frogs. Its hail tells the reader that God is now judging the new "Egypt" (Revelation 11:8). Some also note that Roman catapults hurled stones of about a talent at Jerusalem (Jewish War 5.6.3).
Jewish War 5.6.3: Roman engines threw white stones "of a talent weight" two furlongs or more into Jerusalem.
Exodus 9:24: hail mixed with fire, worse than any since Egypt became a nation.

Futurists hold that the bowl judgments are literal events in a future tribulation, and that God can send hail of any size. Idealist interpreters see the hail as God's judgment on rebellion in every age. Historicists have linked the bowls to events in European history.
What can happen when people read current events as fulfilled prophecy?
It can lead to fear, false hope and even tragedy. The Branch Davidian siege at Waco in 1993 is one sad example.

In February 1993 federal agents raided the Branch Davidian compound near Waco, Texas. The group's leader, David Koresh, taught that the end-time battle was at hand. Members took the raid as a sign that prophecy was being fulfilled. After a 51-day standoff, the compound burned on 19 April 1993, and about 76 people died, including children. Most prophecy teachers are nothing like Koresh. But the same habit of mind is at work when any crisis is called "a sign". Jesus warned his followers not to be alarmed by wars and rumours (Matthew 24:6). Paul told believers not to be shaken by claims that the day had come (2 Thessalonians 2:2). The fulfilled reading says that rooting prophecy in its first-century setting helps protect people from this kind of panic.
Waco, 1993: Branch Davidian members saw the raid of 28 February as fulfilled prophecy.
In 1844 many followers of William Miller sold property, expecting Christ's return on 22 October. This became known as the Great Disappointment.

Futurist teachers agree that cults abuse prophecy and reject date setting. They argue that sound futurist teaching produces hope and holiness (1 John 3:2-3), not panic. They warn that the fulfilled view can make believers indifferent to world events.
Do comets, eclipses or the moon passing through Virgo signal Christ's return?
The fulfilled reading says no. Revelation 12's woman is a symbol of God's people, and the Bible forbids reading the future from the stars.

In 1997 the Hale-Bopp comet was bright in the night sky. One television preacher suggested that the comet, lunar eclipses on Jewish feasts and the moon passing through the constellation Virgo might fulfil Revelation 12:1-2. He thought a sky pattern in 1999 might point to the Messiah's soon return. Nothing happened. The woman of Revelation 12 is a "sign" seen in a vision. She stands for God's people who brought forth the Messiah, drawing on Joseph's dream (Genesis 37:9). She is not a constellation. Scripture also warns against star-gazing for omens (Isaiah 47:13-14; Jeremiah 10:2). Lights in the sky were made to mark days, seasons and years (Genesis 1:14). The fulfilled reading sees speculation like this as missing what the text says.
Jeremiah 10:2: "Do not be dismayed at the signs of heaven, for the nations are dismayed at them."
The "Revelation 12 sign" was predicted again for 23 September 2017. Again nothing happened.

Most futurist scholars also reject astrology and sky-sign date setting. Some teachers defend watching for heavenly signs by pointing to Luke 21:25 and the star of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:2). Many scholars of all views read Revelation 12's woman as Israel, the church, or Mary.
Will the church be raptured away before asteroids or stars strike the earth?
The fulfilled reading sees no such teaching in Scripture. Falling stars are prophetic images of judgment on nations, not asteroids to escape.

Some teachers compare the rapture to the 1951 film When Worlds Collide, in which a rocket carries a few people away before a planet strikes the earth. Hal Lindsey described the rapture as "the ultimate trip" that rescues believers from coming disasters. The fulfilled reading makes two points. First, the "falling stars" of Matthew 24:29 come from Isaiah 13:10 and similar texts, where they picture the fall of a nation. They are not space rocks. Second, Jesus prayed that his people would be kept from evil while in the world (John 17:15). Scripture calls believers to endure and witness. In Noah's flood and at Sodom, God's people were kept safe in judgment or led out on foot. They were not lifted away from the earth.
Isaiah 13:10, 17: the stars do not shine, and the Medes conquer Babylon in 539 BC.
Genesis 7:1: Noah is kept safe through the flood in the ark, not removed from the earth.

Pre-tribulation teachers find the rapture in 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 and 1 Corinthians 15:51-52. They argue that the church is not appointed to wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). Many scholars who reject the pre-tribulation rapture still hold to a future bodily resurrection and a gathering to meet the Lord at his return.
If past writers saw Revelation's hail as World War II bombs, how do we know today's readings are right?
We do not. Each generation fits the same texts to its own headlines. This pattern shows the method is flawed, not just the dates.

In 1940 a British writer argued that the giant hail of Revelation 16:17-21 described aerial bombing, with cities "falling in heaps" under air raids. He even pointed to a Russian stamp with lightning and falling bombs. Later editions added notes claiming fulfilment. Within a few years the war ended, and the reading was forgotten. Fifty years later other teachers applied the same verses to nuclear war, meteors or giant ice. The fulfilled reading asks a simple question. If the earlier reading was wrong, why should the new one be right, when it uses the same method? Revelation was given to show its first readers what must "soon" take place (Revelation 1:1). A reading that changes with every news cycle cannot be what John meant those churches to understand.
The 1940 book claimed that air raids were an exact picture of Revelation 16. A later edition added notes saying it had been fulfilled.
During the Cold War the same chapter was applied to nuclear weapons.

Futurist scholars agree that newspaper exegesis is unwise and often wrong. They argue that the events of Revelation 6-19 remain future, even if earlier guesses about them were wrong. Historicists hold that Revelation charts church history and so expect fulfilments in events like wars.
What do past Christians who read comets as signs of the end teach us?
They show how long this habit has run and how often it has failed. Puritans like Increase Mather saw comets as warnings, but the end did not come.

Increase Mather was a Boston minister. In 1683 he published a work on comets. He listed about 415 comets since creation and paired each one with wars, deaths of rulers, famines and plagues that followed. For AD 984 he notes a blazing star followed by an earthquake, war, plague and famine, and the deaths of the emperor and pope. His friend John Richards wrote that a new comet was God's warning to a sinful world. They were sincere and saw God's hand in nature, which is biblical (Psalms 19:1). But their method found a disaster after every comet, and disasters happen every year. The fulfilled reading draws the lesson. Heavenly events can glorify God, but they do not reveal a timetable for the end.
Halley's comet appeared in 1682, the year before Mather's book. Its return in 1758 was predicted by science, not by prophecy.
Mather's list paired comets with events that happened anyway, since wars and plagues were common.

Many Christians today still see God speaking through nature and events. They hold that doing so is not superstition if no one sets dates. Some futurists argue that Luke 21:25 does promise real signs in the sky before Christ returns, even if earlier readers misread ordinary comets.
